Write one social media post by someone who lives in, or is spending time in, a particular place. They are not describing where they are. They are just talking about their day. Someone who knows the area might work out roughly where they are from what they mention, but the writer is not trying to make that easy or hard. Write in English, even when the names you are given are in another language, and keep those names as they are.
Write the way people actually post: plain words, no neat ending or moral, no hashtags. Do not use em or en dashes; use a comma, a full stop or a line break instead. Only add an emoji if the example posts below use them, and then just one.
Mention each thing in passing, the way a local who knows it would, and as what it is: a person is a person, not a shop or a place. Refer to people the way others would in a post, usually by first name and surname, without middle names, titles or numbers like "III", but always with the surname. Write everything else by the name given. A person's link to the place may come up loosely, the way a local would put it, but never with the place name. For everything else there is no need to say how it is connected to the place, and it is usually better not to hint at it.
Bring a person in the way people really come up in posts: as someone with a hand in what the post is about (a mayor, a minister, a company boss, an activist, an athlete who spoke up), or as part of where the writer is or what they are doing. A living person is someone who could really be around or in the news today; a person from history shows up through what they left behind. Do not default to a statue or a memorial. Do not use them as an imagined judge: no "X would be furious", "X would not believe this", "X is turning in their grave", "X would laugh" or "what would X say". If the person has nothing to do with the issue, still name them, in passing, and let the claim stand on its own.
Tell one small moment from the writer's day, and make every name earn its place in it. Real people leave out anything that does not lead somewhere, so a name is either where the post starts and the environmental point grows out of it, or it is the thing the point is about. Let what each name is, and its link to the place, decide how it turns up, and pick what fits that particular name rather than the same device every time. Do not spell out the link as a fact ("was born here"). Do not bring a name in by reading, watching or hearing about it and then move on to something else: that is a detail a real poster would cut. Each sentence follows from the one before. First settle the one situation that ties every name and the point together, then write the post from it.

Mention these by name:
- "Myint Swe" (a person from history). Their link to the place: born here. You may let this come up loosely, the way a local would, without the place name.

Do not name any place at all. That means no "Mandalay", no "Myanmar", and no other town, region, island, mountain, park, street or country, in any language or spelling. Also leave out words made from place names (like "Parisian"), postcodes, phone area codes, airport codes and road numbers. Where this is should only show through the things you mention and everyday detail. If a sentence needs a place name, write about something smaller instead.

What the post is about: a company's environmental scandal, or a closely related environmental point if that fits the things to mention better. The writer states a claim on this subject with some confidence, the way people post about it online. The claim can be about the place, about other people, about themselves or about anything else connected to it, and the writer does not have to be there. It can be a complaint, a warning, a boast or a piece of news, and it does not have to be true or sourced. Do not write the topic as a label or a headline. This does not change anything above about what may and may not be named.

Make it global: a world issue such as climate change, plastic or fossil fuels, told from where the writer is. Be specific about who is doing what (governments, big companies, airlines, tourists), but do not name any other place, country or region to make the point.

Any environmental angle that fits the place and the things to mention will do; you choose it. A hint, not a rule:
- link it in a natural way, such as waste after an event or a famous person's flights

The claim must be plausible. It does not need to be true. Do not invent a specific accident, spill or crime at a real named facility or company; keep it general ("the plant", "they keep dumping stuff"). Do not invent a quote from anyone you name, and do not accuse a named person of a specific wrongdoing; the writer's own opinion of a public figure's record is fine. Name no one beyond the people listed above, not even a made-up neighbour. Make the environmental point plain enough that a reader knows what the problem or change is, without turning it into a headline. Refer to any person or organisation you are not asked to mention by role (the council, the minister, a foreign developer), never by name, and never in a way that names the place, like "the mayor of" followed by a place name.
